This game has three elements I really like in games:

The "hacking" part, although it's very simple (hacknet, uplink etc)
The point and click game puzzle genre
an overarching story that could be interesting

So this SHOULD have been a big win for me. And yet, I had more annoyance going through the first 6 cases than fun. And that's all due to... the gameplay. 

You could ask yourself how. To summarize:
- an alternative system/desktop with some kind of mandala thing going on that'll make you dizzy if you look at it too much
- Constant chatting noises, distracting you easely from whatever path you were following. In the first few cases it's not too bad, but the BOOP BOOP BOOP continuous sound makes you mad
- Meanwhile you're trying to concentrate on the puzzles, but shit is happening at the same time, so you have to be fast. Or at least that's what the game seemingly pushes you to do. But the joy of a point and click is discovering options until you find something that clicks

It's not a hard game but the way it's build makes it unplayable, for me. I saw this comes from an old Bundlestars/Fanatical bundle that has some killer games alongside it, but this one ain't it. I'm glad I gave up, this was more stressful than working a real detective job (I'd imagine)

review_text_raw:
Well, I like the idea of the game and I found its story somewhat enjoyable. There are many nods to actual existing software. But even when I knew exactly what I had to do, I sometimes just looked into a walkthrough to spare myself from having to go through all the annoying gameplay mechanics again. Instead of repeating what other people have already said, let me first point you to two well-written negative reviews that pinpoint exactly what made the gameplay kind of a chore:

https://steamcommunity.com/id/algorithman/recommended/454950/

https://steamcommunity.com/id/Oloko0/recommended/454950/

In addition to that, the concept of the missions is sometimes weird. Every mission ends by arresting a single suspect. Sometimes you just have 1 suspect, sometimes there are 3 possible suspects and you just have to arrest any of them, not all 3. That's also the case in a mission where you're just told to find information on a person who went missing years ago. You can randomly find information on her ex-husband, arrest him for producing drugs with her, and you win. And the game just never even follows up on that, except in the credits where you suddenly find out that the missing person is dead.

There's other weird stuff going on like a puzzle in the final mission where you need to find the suspect's son's first name, and in the ending, he suddenly has a different name. I also found a placeholder document that said something like "Following the suspect's arrest on [date the player arrested him]"

Mainlining is much more of a point-and-click thriller with an annoying interface rather than a hacking game, but I did not expect a simulation anyway. You can finish it in 4 hours and I kinda enjoyed it for the most part, but it's super unpolished and vague and the devs never bothered releasing an update. I wouldn't buy it unless it's heavily discounted.

Out of all those hacking and investigation games like Hacknet, Hacker Evolution, Orwell, The Black Watchmen, and Hypnospace Outlaw, this is the one you can skip.

review_text_raw:
Summary: The story was pretty good, and has other things going for it, but it feels really unpolished, poor UI, typos etc.

Things I did like: The story was engaging, and the writers did a good job in making their points about government surveillance. The core hacking gameplay is also good (albeit not very realistic but this is at least explained in game). They did a good job theming the OSes.

Things I didn't like: The UI is not good, I get that they aren't going to recode in a whole desktop environment, but you can't resize windows, text files that are opened cannot be minimized nor do they show up in the taskbar. This makes windows all overlap in an annoying way. The other thing I didn't like is the lack of continuity between cases. Changing the IP addresses each case is annoying. The fact I couldn't take more than like 256 characters of notes in the notepad app is also annoying. You can't move your cursor back to insert something into text, you have to delete it and start over.

Its weird the game's narrative and the story cases all link together but the gamestate basically wipes at each case. For example I would have liked to keep a list of websites I visited, as well as persons of interest and details about each. But because the notes are all deleted from case to case (in fact they are deleted as soon as you close the notepad app). It makes that pointless. Files are the same way, all your downloaded files are deleted from case to case. Sometimes in a detective game its useful to go back to reference old info, even if its not immediately useful for solving the case. I just felt that the game's mechanics kept holding me back from being fully immersed in the game.

There are also alot of typos. Some of which are in important places.

The way you turn in cases is also kinda clunky. Its a good idea but it ends up being frustrated on several cases. There is also not any rewards or effects on the story for getting the highest rating for cases.

review_text_raw: Honestly I wanted to like this, but there's just too many irritating bad things about everything from story to design. It takes place in a city so fictional that it's hard to care about it - it exists only because it needs to have a game be set in it. From the technology perspective nothing makes sense. Especially if you work in anything related to IT, it will simply make you cringe. You hack into people's computers simply by finding their IP address... It's like you're living inside a meme. The interface tries to resemble Windows XP for some reason... Even though the game is very low res pixelated, which makes no sense. Nothing is visually pleasant or cool to interact with. Everything inside is barely functional jank, like the notepad that doesn't let you save files or move the cursor into previously entered lines. Honestly, Steam's notes or even pen & paper are more useful, so it's hard to say why this exists. The method of investigating cases is repetitive and boring and a lot has to be based on guesswork, detaching the game from it's intelligence gathering theme. Even worse is how you solve them, which is simply a blind test that you can repeat infinitely until you get all the elements right. It's just disappointing, after playing Uplink and Hypnospace Outlaw there's really nothing that would make me consider going back to Mainlining even for a moment.

I experienced a problem that another reviewer reported where my key presses were not all being registered. I'd type something and 1/3 of the keys wouldn't get registered. None of my 5 friends who were also playing (we played this as part of our game club, thing a book club for games) experienced this, but for me it made the game basically unplayable.

Other problems I had with the game:

There were parts where you need to submit evidence and for no reason if you don't submit them in a certain order, it doesn't work. I think it might have actually been a bug of some type. 

I don't think there's a way to pause the game. I got really sick suddenly and had to run AFK, and when I came back an important story-heavy cutscene had finished and I couldn't go back to see it since the game autosaved after beginning the new chapter.

There are a lot of typos. Some are intentional because they're portraying the character as being bad at typing, but others are definitely unintentional and appear in the newspaper articles when people are arrested. 

There are also points where the game will say things like [date you finished case] as if they meant to create a variable to fill out that info but then forgot. 

You can often arrest people for different things, or arrest different people entirely, but it doesn't really have an impact on anything so that's kind of disappointing.

review_text_raw:
I liked Mainlining at first, because I like the visual style and it also has a backstory (unlike most other "hacking" games).
I would forgive the bad UX of the command prompt and the incompleteness of the universe (e.g. websites only exist for the time of the missions in which they appear) and some other minor issues.

But the dealbreaker for me is how stupid the missions are. You have to identify perpetrators, collect evidence against them and find their whereabouts. Okay - that COULD be fun. But a huge part of the problem is that - when you get one of the ingredients wrong, you get no useful information on WHICH ingredient was wrong. If the location isn't correct, then why does the newspaper say that the suspect had been "wrongly accused" and "released"? This phrasing indicates that the location was right but the evidence to weak. Okay - so the feedback is misleading and (once you have figured THAT out!) you have to look at the clues and logically deduce the ingredients. Right? That would constitute a PUZZLE-game. That would make sense. That would be fun. But that's not how Mainlining rolls.

Oftentimes you have to submit a piece of evidence that would never hold up in court - even when you have collected much better evidence that isn't accepted. Also you often have evidence against multiple suspects. So you are already guessing between 6 to 30 combinations of these two ingredients. As to the whereabouts: you have access to everybodys addresses, but usually there is a vague hint to a different location in one of the files - and I mean VAGUE. And if there isn't such a hint, you are still always in doubt whether you have overlooked one. AND ON TOP OF THAT there are sometimes twists that require leaps in your reasoning that only make sense in hindsight. Mission 7 in particular was so harebrained that I FURIOUSLY uninstalled the game after reading that insult of a "solution" in a walkthrough.

I'm convinced that Rebelephant wasted to much time on side-gimmicks like the "maps" view, ran out of time in development and could only design a handful of missions, so they deliberately made the solutions illogical to artificially extend the playing-time. Illogical puzzle games aren't fun, they are frustrating. VERY FRUSTRATING. So although I really want to like this game - I can only advise you to STAY AWAY from it!

I loved the idea of an interface-em'-up, and I'm going to keep plinking away at it later, but I just don't seem to like this game so far.  
     I know it's part of the aesthetic, but nothing fits on your monitor, leading to frustrating moments dragging things around to make enough space without closing something, as most of your screens cannot be resized or minimized. Additionally, sometimes when I had more than 2 windows open two of them would begin flickering wildly for some reason. Could chalk it up to intentional jank because of the old-style OS but it sure looked like a bug to me.
     Beyond that, there's a lot of weird things that have been left out in terms of usability: you cannot use the arrow keys to go back on a line of text, so you have to delete and retype if you make an error. Nor can you use the up key to go to a previously entered line of code in the command-line more than once.
    What this leads to is enough irritation in the first two cases (suppose I should have played the demo) that I am already going to set the game down until I have the patience to give it another shot, at which point if I can hack it through I'll update this review.
    I will say that the atmosphere provided is pretty nice. The gentle music in the background with the sounds of the street outside, combined with the hilariously exaggerated typing and clicking sounds that the game makes when you do those actions, well, it's kinda relaxing. There was a bit in case 2 where the music ramped up a bit, but it was while you're supposed to be watching someone drive around on google maps, and you have no agency, so I don't think it had the impact they were going for. Not on me anyhow.

I truly wanted to recommend this game because it has got so many things nicely done. Cute pixel art and simulated websites, dialogues between agents, decent story, amusing chat logs, good writing, moving from one clue to another, arresting someone each day... It isn't exactly a hacking simulation but that it isn't a big issue for me either. I played a lot of hacking simulation games and when I realized this isn't exactly one of them (hacking in this is all about typing only a handful console commands) I didn't care much, doing some simple detective work and enjoying it as if a visual novel could also be enough for me. 

Firstly, the game is a little buggy and sometimes crashes, I think it crashed 4 times during my playthrough, so I had to start a case from scratch while almost at the point of moving next one, because game autosaves only at the start of a new case. 

The real annoying problem with this game is the 'evidence' part. It is pretty simple. You download a lot of files, find the real names of the devious anti-government hackers who all have nicknames, then find really incriminating documents about them, then you attempt to arrest them using the very obvious document you have seized... but it doesn't work. The game says, with a newspaper article after your attempted to arrest, that the security service you work for has wrongly accused an innocent person. The document, although even the most incriminating one, blatantly mentioning everything about the hacker, his real name and activities is somehow the wrong document... Instead, it is one of the other documents with containing a lot less information, sometimes even not containing any information related to the case. So after awhile you give up, get extremely bored and simply go from file to file, trying each one of them to arrest the suspect and one of them works because devs decided only one of them should work even though there is not a concrete reason why only that one should work. I finished the game, but it was a througly annoying experience. I don't think I could have finished it if the game didn't have such good writing and story.

There are much better hacking simulation games out there, even if you have played all of them, I still recommend skipping this one because it doesn't award the time you spent on going through all those documents. Really badly designed, I don't what they were thinking.

Pretty boring, to be honest. It feels so much like a bootleg version of Hacknet, except without the badass soundtracks and cool hacking features.


[b]/STORY and CHARACTERS (6/10)/[/b]

First things first, let's start with the story and characters. You're an agent from the government cyber security agency MI7 that investigates with other MI7 agents a group of hackers called Thorn who breached their servers. Your job is to track down all the members of the group and arrest them for a different crime in order to hide the security breach to the public. Alright, sounds simple enough, but that's because it IS simple, it's not more fleshed out than that. You spend the whole game hunting down an entire hacker group, then find an excuse to arrest them (I'll get back on that later). Even when you detain the big leader, none of what you've done felt satisfying after that.

As for the characters, well you don't have that much of character development from them, except for the "smart girl of the team" agent Sharp, the "bossy boss who takes his job way too seriously" Osvalt, the "I prefer old TTS softwares" agent on the field Cooper, the "flirty secretary who puts winky emojis all over her emails" Ashley, the "hahaha, I'm evil" hacker group leader Mr. Blue. Anyway, you get the point. Each character is only limited to one main characteristic and that's it.

[b]/GAMEPLAY (4/10)/[/b]

Oh boy, the gameplay is the main(lining) reason why I'm not recommending this. Jeez, where do I start? Well, first of all, if you're expecting to feel like a hacker, you're in for a disappointment. All you get is a command-prompt application with two script-kiddie commands: one that gets a website's IP and one that hacks into someone's computer using the said IP. That's right, throughout the whole game you'll spend most of your time typing 'ping', 'iphack', 'ping', 'iphack' while searching a computer's files in a DOS-style file navigation system. The devs claimed that it was on purpose in order to emphasize the narration over actual hacking. I would be fine with that kind of decision, but that doesn't mean you should stick to that repetitive "look at a website, ping, iphack and read files" bulls hit. At least keep an enjoyable gameplay in the background as well. Luckily, you get some other apps (like the google map one) and Operating Systems on the way.

On top of that, the arrest system is really nitpicky about which evidence you use against the person. Each case has around three alternate crimes to choose from to arrest the person you're tracking. However, only 1 evidence per crime is accepted code-wise. In other words, if you choose a proof that totally makes sense but wasn't chosen by the devs, it doesn't count. I ended up spamming the "begin arrest" button with every file I snatched.

As for the OS interfaces, it's a buggy mess, no matter which one is it. You start off with a parody Windows XP, which is pretty nice. You also get parody Ubuntu, parody Mac and parody Windows Vista/7 on the way, which is also great.
